facts.claim: "So Damn Lucky" appears on Taylor McCall's album Black Powder Soul, released September 24, 2021 on Black Powder Soul Records. The track runs 4:03.
"So Damn Lucky" was written by Taylor McCall and Sean McConnell.
Sean McConnell produced the album Black Powder Soul, which includes this song.
McCall and McConnell met for the first time at the co-write that produced "So Damn Lucky". Holler describes the song as a dynamic acoustic charmer.
McCall said the words for "So Damn Lucky" came to him while he was walking up the stairs at his first writing session with Sean McConnell.
McCall called "So Damn Lucky" the keystone of the album Black Powder Soul. It was released as a single on July 22, 2021, ahead of the album.

The Discogs credits for Black Powder Soul say it was recorded by Sean McConnell at Silent Desert Studio in Nolensville, TN. Justin Tocket mixed it at Dockside Studio, and Brian Lucey mastered it at Magic Garden Mastering.
McCall said the album sessions took place over two weeks in McConnell's home studio.

Black Powder Soul is McCall's full-length debut, and it has 14 tracks. It opens with a prologue featuring the voice of his late grandfather. McCall says it explores good and evil and the importance of faith in the darkest of times.
McCall is a South Carolina native who got his first guitar at age seven. He is described as an avid outdoorsman and fisherman with self-taught guitar styles. He had released EPs before this album.

draft:
**So Damn Lucky** opens with a man giving himself orders. He tells himself to sober up and settle down. Then he admits that the person he's talking to should have left by now and hasn't. The song never explains why they stayed. Taylor McCall doesn't seem to know either, and that confusion is the whole emotional engine. This is a love song written from a low opinion of yourself, where gratitude and disbelief are the same feeling.

The verses fill in the family history fast. "I'm just like my old man," McCall sings, and in the next breath his mother is trying her best and his partner is a lot like her. It's a quick sketch of a pattern repeating, and the narrator sees exactly which side of it he's on. The best image comes later: "I'm a coin on the ground." It's small and a little ashamed. Something dropped and overlooked, and someone bending down anyway. Then there's the last verse, where he loves her "in my way" and allows, "I may choke on my pride." Pride and humility sit right next to each other and never settle. He knows he's lucky and still can't quite say it straight, which is why the title phrase keeps coming back like something he's repeating to make it real.

The chorus leans on the old scripture about love being patient and kind, credited offhandedly to "somebody." That casual nod fits a record McCall says is about good and evil and faith in the darkest of times. It was his full-length debut, and he called this song its keystone.

The sound matches the confession. A fingerpicked acoustic guitar carries it, with bass walking underneath. Drums come in on a plain kick, snare, and hi-hat beat that never pushes. The tempo is unhurried and the groove is relaxed with a melancholy lean. McCall's voice has a rasp to it, and he sings without ornament, like he's telling you rather than performing for you. The room is dry and the mix is clean, close enough to hear the grain.

That closeness has a backstory. McCall wrote the song with Sean McConnell at their first meeting. McCall said the words came to him while he was walking up the stairs to that session. McConnell went on to produce *Black Powder Soul* over two weeks in his home studio in Nolensville, Tennessee. Holler called it a dynamic acoustic charmer. It sits in the Americana and alt-country tradition, the kind of plain-spoken song that runs from front porches to Nashville writing rooms. What it adds is the shame tucked inside the thank-you.

It sticks because it gives you the feeling of being loved more than you think you've earned, and of not being able to stop counting your luck.

factCheck.claim: The song opens with the narrator telling himself to sober up and settle down; the other person 'should have left by now and hasn't'.
factCheck.note: Matches the opening lines: 'Sober up / Settle down / You should be gone by now / But your not'. All three listening passes describe a male voice.

factCheck.claim: 'Taylor McCall doesn't seem to know either'
factCheck.note: The confusion belongs to the narrator in the lyrics. Changed to 'the narrator' so the artist isn't credited with feelings the words don't show.

factCheck.claim: Quote: "I'm just like my old man"; mother trying her best; partner a lot like her
factCheck.note: Matches 'I'm just like my old man / Mama tries best she can / You're like her a lot'.

factCheck.claim: Quote: "I'm a coin on the ground."
factCheck.note: Exact lyric. 'Comes later' is supported by the lyric order.

factCheck.claim: Quote: "in my way", plus "I may choke on my pride", described as 'the last verse'
factCheck.note: Both lines are in the lyrics, but the song's last section is a repeated chorus, so 'last verse' was changed to 'a later verse'. 'In my way' is now paraphrased to keep the quotes to three.

factCheck.claim: The chorus leans on 'the old scripture' about love being patient and kind, credited to 'somebody'
factCheck.note: The lyric says 'Somebody said love is patient and kind'. Nothing in the packet ties it to scripture, so that was dropped and the line is described as a familiar saying.

factCheck.claim: McCall says the record is about good and evil and faith in the darkest of times; it was his full-length debut; he called the song its keystone
Fingerpicked acoustic guitar, walking bass, kick/snare/hi-hat drums

Pass 1 says the drums add rhythmic drive, so this isn't supported.

factCheck.claim: Unhurried tempo, relaxed groove with a melancholy lean
factCheck.note: Passes 1 and 3 say relaxed and slightly melancholic, and pass 2 says relaxed. Tempo is moderate to slow in all three.

factCheck.claim: Raspy voice, sung without ornament, conversational
factCheck.note: Slightly raspy in all passes. Unadorned (pass 1) and conversational (pass 2) agree.

factCheck.claim: Room is dry and the mix is clean
factCheck.note: Dry is supported by passes 1 and 3. 'Clean' is contradicted by pass 3 (raw, unpolished), so it was removed.

factCheck.claim: McCall wrote the song with Sean McConnell at their first meeting; words came to him walking up the stairs to that session
factCheck.note: Backed by the Holler and Sound in the Signals facts.

factCheck.claim: McConnell produced Black Powder Soul over two weeks in his home studio in Nolensville, Tennessee
factCheck.note: McConnell produced the album, and McCall said the sessions took two weeks in McConnell's home studio. Discogs says it was recorded at Silent Desert Studio in Nolensville, TN. The claim is now split along those lines rather than equating the home studio with the Nolensville location.
